questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ Computing $A-6I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{3}.$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm, we obtain the third column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=9.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2}.$ 

Now, we need to find eigenvectors that correspond to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Computing $A-4I,$ we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are orthogonal. Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=7.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Computing $A-I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{1}={v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

and we find ${e}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{1}}{‖{e}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6} \\ \frac{\sqrt{6}}{3} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
